accuracy.evidence: Checked against basic sound physics at an early-years level: a harder hit, stronger shake or bigger breath gives larger vibrations and a louder sound, a still shaker makes no sound, and bigger bells ring lower while tiny bells ring higher. The adult notes add the honest caveat that blowing harder into a recorder or toy trumpet can raise the pitch as well as the volume.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the confusions reported for young children: treating high as loud and low as quiet (the squeaky toy item, the bell prediction and the Loud, because it is high option), believing big instruments are always loud whatever the force, and treating fast tapping as the same as hard tapping. Each has its own wrong option and feedback line.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagloud lab is about force and sound: a loud and quiet sorting tray, a drumstick whose lift height sets the bang, a shaker for a sleeping baby versus a band, a toy trumpet blown softly or hard, and a big bell against a tiny bell with a drawn wave for low and high. Highest shingle overlap with any other flag lab is 6.6 percent (flag_skip, shared shell helpers).

lab_teaches.evidence: Every step pairs one action with one result so the cause is plain: lifting the stick higher gives a bigger bang, the shaker job switches between gentle for baby and hard for the band, and the trumpet task asks for soft then hard. The bell step deliberately keeps loudness the same and changes only size, so high and low stay a separate idea.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked before acting: how to make a loud sound on the drum (gently or hard), how to blow the trumpet so Dad hears from far away, and whether the big bell or the tiny bell rings high. The done message after each task restates the locked guess and says whether the action confirmed it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions rotate their option order, and every wrong option has its own reply, for example A still shaker makes no sound, things must move to make a sound, and High is not the same as loud, a tiny bell is high and it can ring loud or quiet. A run counter and Another button keep the practice going.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use very short words and sentences (Bang a drum hard. BOOM! That is loud.), well under the family reading limit, and the lab prompts are under ten words each for three and four year olds. The adult notes use the Development Matters wording for the Understanding the World and Expressive Arts and Design strands.

no_filler.evidence: Each adult paragraph does one job: where the topic sits in the EYFS and Year 4 science, the cause and effect idea plus the pitch caveat, the named mistakes, and what the lab steps do. The family tip gives a concrete pots-and-pans game with the hidden-instrument guessing task from the topic evidence.

mobile.evidence: The young layout gives 56 pixel buttons, every action works by tap as well as drag, and the drum lift can be set with Gentle tap and Hard hit buttons. Screens on iPhone 13 and Android in light and dark themes keep the instruments, meter and bell waves inside the canvas with no overlapping text.

accessibility.evidence: Sound is optional, so every result is also shown as words and a loudness meter, the canvas aria-label is updated with each spoken line, and the answer buttons sit in a labelled group with a polite live status. The browser gate ran axe in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations.
